transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Honestly, I’m here because things at work have gotten kind of out of hand. I do maintenance and repair stuff, and I keep forgetting callbacks I was supposed to make, work orders I said I’d handle, even little follow-ups I promised people—and then suddenly it’s not little anymore, it’s a whole pile.

My supervisor’s been on me about it, and they basically sent me here because I’m trying to move up, and if I keep dropping things like this, I’m going to lose that chance. It’s embarrassing, because I mean to do it, I really do. I’ll tell someone, “Yeah, I’ll call you back,” and then something else happens, or I go to grab a part, and—well, you know how one thing turns into another. But now it’s causing real problems.

Would you say you've struggled with this kind of forgetfulness and losing track of tasks for as long as you can remember, even back in school, or is this something that's really only become a problem more recently?

Oh, no, this goes way back. I mean, work has made it more obvious because there’s more on the line, but I remember being like this in grade school too.

Teachers used to say I was bright, but I was always losing papers or forgetting to turn something in, or I’d only do part of the directions because I missed the rest somehow. My desk was always a mess too—well, everybody’s desk was a little messy, but mine was the one where the permission slip would disappear and then turn up weeks later. And they were always reminding me to finish classwork, like I’d start it and then somehow not get to the end unless someone came by and nudged me. So yeah, it’s not new. It’s just catching up with me harder now.
Do you often feel restless, fidgety, or find it hard to sit still, or do you tend to act or speak impulsively—like interrupting others or blurting things out—in daily life?

Um… I don’t know, not really? I mean, I can get antsy if I’m sitting too long, like anybody, especially in those waiting room chairs—those things are awful, and I always wonder who picks them because nobody’s comfortable in them.

But the interrupting or blurting stuff… I’m not sure. I don’t think of myself as, like, jumping out of my skin all the time. At work I’m usually moving around anyway, so it’s hard to tell what I’d be like sitting still all day. I guess I’d have to think about that more.
Thinking back to when you were a kid, did teachers or family ever say you had trouble staying seated, talked excessively, or acted before thinking things through?

I’m not really sure. I mean, I don’t remember anyone making a big deal about me being out of my seat or talking too much. My brother was the loud one in the house, so if anybody got told to sit down and stop climbing on stuff, it was usually him.

I was more… I don’t know, I’d get in trouble for other things, but as far as acting before thinking, I’m sure I did dumb kid stuff. Everybody did. Like one time we tried to make a ramp for bikes out of old plywood behind the garage, and my mom still brings that up—though that might’ve just been normal kid stupidity, not anything special.

So, no, I don’t have a clear memory of teachers saying that about me. It was more like I was always being reminded or corrected, but I can’t really say it was for not staying seated or talking too much.
Outside of work, do you notice similar problems now—like losing track of personal tasks, misplacing things, or forgetting appointments at home or in your personal life?

Yeah, I mean… it’s not just work, but work is where it’s gotten me in real trouble. What brought me in is I keep forgetting scheduled callbacks and work orders and even little follow-ups I told people I’d handle. And then they pile up, and once they’re piled up it’s like—well, you know when you have a junk drawer and you swear you’re going to clean it, but then suddenly there’s batteries and old keys and takeout menus from a place that closed five years ago? It kind of gets like that, except with actual responsibilities.

And now work sent me here because it’s gotten bad enough that I could mess up my chance at moving up. That’s the part that scares me, honestly. I’ve worked hard, and I don’t want to lose my shot because I can’t keep track of what I said I’d do.
Have you been feeling persistently down, anxious, or unusually stressed lately that might be affecting your concentration, or does this forgetfulness happen even when your mood feels fine?

I mean… I don’t think it’s only when I’m upset or stressed. Work is stressful now because of it, if that makes sense, like it became stressful after I kept dropping things.

What brought me in is I keep forgetting scheduled callbacks, work orders, and even basic follow-ups I told people I’d handle. And then it piles up, and once it piles up it’s like I don’t even know where to start. Work finally sent me here because they’re worried, and honestly I’m worried too, because I don’t want this to ruin my chance at moving up.
Do you find that you're easily distracted by things going on around you—like noises, other people talking, or things happening nearby—when you're trying to focus on a task?

Yeah, definitely. Like I’ll start a digital work order thinking, okay, I’ve got this, I’m reading the notes, I know what needs doing… and then halfway through, some noise happens or somebody walks by or I think about the next job, and suddenly I realize I don’t actually know what I just read.

It’s embarrassing because I’m looking right at it, you know? The screen is right there, and my eyes are moving, but my brain has gone off somewhere else. Then I have to go back and reread it, sometimes more than once. And it’s not even always a big distraction—sometimes it’s just a sound in the hallway or hearing part of someone else’s conversation, and I’m gone.
Do you often have trouble organizing tasks or activities—like figuring out what to do first, planning out your day, or keeping track of steps needed to finish a job—even when you're not distracted?

I’m not totally sure how to separate that from being distracted, honestly. Like… if I’m trying to plan something, there’s usually something else going on anyway, or I’ve already got three things in my head.

I guess I do get kind of tangled up with where to start sometimes, but I don’t know if that’s “organizing” exactly or just me making it harder than it needs to be. Like at home, I’ll look at a pile of stuff and think, okay, laundry first, no dishes first, no wait I need to move that box—and then somehow I’m standing there thinking about whether we still have that old cooler in the garage. Which is probably not what you asked.

So… yeah, maybe, but I’m not sure I can give you a clean answer on that.
Do you find yourself avoiding, putting off, or dreading tasks that require a lot of sustained mental effort—like paperwork, detailed reports, or planning—even when you know they’re important?

I don’t know if I’d call it dreading exactly. I mean, paperwork is never my favorite thing, but whose is, right? My sister actually likes forms, which I’ve never understood—she’ll sit there with little folders and labels and everything.

For me, I guess if something looks like it’s going to take a lot of thinking, I might kind of circle around it before I start, but I’m not sure if that’s avoiding it or just… trying to get myself ready. Sometimes I tell myself I’ll do it after one other thing, and then the day gets away from me.

But I don’t know. I wouldn’t say I’ve really noticed it as a pattern, if that’s what you mean.

Um… I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I don’t really keep track of my sleep like that. Some nights feel fine, some mornings I’m still kind of dragging, but I don’t know if that’s sleep or just… mornings, you know?

Were you asking like insomnia, or waking up a lot, or something else? Because I’d have to think about it more. I haven’t really noticed a clear pattern.

Would you say these attention and forgetfulness issues have also caused noticeable problems in your relationships or social life—like friends or family feeling frustrated with you for forgetting things or not following through?

Yeah… I mean, socially, I’m not sure that’s where I’d say it shows the most. My family gets annoyed sometimes, sure, but the bigger thing right now is work.

It’s gotten kind of serious there. I’ve got this backlog that keeps following me around, and tenants have been complaining because things don’t get finished or followed up on the way they’re supposed to. And now there’s a safety review on my record, which… I hate even saying that out loud.

I’ve been trying to move up, you know, not stay in the same maintenance role forever, and I’m scared this is going to mess up the promotion path I’ve been working toward. So maybe that’s not exactly what you asked about friends and family, but that’s the part that’s really causing problems.
Do you regularly drink alcohol, use any recreational drugs, or consume a lot of caffeine, and do you think any of that might be affecting your focus or memory?

I don’t think so? I mean, I’m not really sure what counts as “a lot” of caffeine. I’ll have coffee, but then some days at work somebody brings one of those huge gas station cups and everybody acts like that’s normal, so I don’t know where the line is.

Alcohol… I wouldn’t say it’s something I’ve connected to my focus. Recreational drugs, no—well, I mean, not like something that’s part of my life. I haven’t really sat down and compared “this day I drank coffee” to “this day I forgot things,” if that’s what you mean.

My focus problems feel like they’re just kind of there, but I don’t know. Maybe I should pay more attention to that.

Can you recall a specific instance from before you were about 12 years old—like a missed homework assignment or a forgotten school project—where this kind of forgetfulness actually caused a real consequence, like a bad grade or getting in trouble?

Yeah, I can remember that kind of thing from grade school. I don’t know if I can pull up one perfect example with the exact grade and teacher, but I remember teachers saying I was bright, like I understood things, but I was always losing papers or forgetting to turn things in.

There were times I’d do part of an assignment and miss a whole section because I didn’t catch all the directions, and then I’d get marked down or have to stay in at recess or something to finish it. And I remember needing reminders to finish classwork, like I’d just… not get it completed unless someone came back around and told me to keep going.

It’s funny, I can picture the desks and those paper folders more than the actual assignment. I was always cramming loose papers into them and then somehow the one I needed would disappear. But yeah, this was way before work stress or anything like that. It was back in school.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure how to separate that from being distracted, honestly. Like… if I’m trying to plan something, there’s usually something else going on anyway, or I’ve already got three things in my head.

I guess I do get kind of tangled up with where to start sometimes, but I don’t know if that’s “organizing” exactly or just me making it harder than it needs to be. Like at home, I’ll look at a pile of stuff and think, okay, laundry first, no dishes first, no wait I need to move that box—and then somehow I’m standing there thinking about whether we still have that old cooler in the garage. Which is probably not what you asked.

So… yeah, maybe, but I’m not sure I can give you a clean answer on that.

inference.note: Continued endorsement of inattentive symptoms (distractibility, disorganization, forgetfulness) with childhood onset, while hyperactive-impulsive symptoms remain absent, supporting predominantly inattentive presentation rather than combined type ADHD. No evidence supports mood or anxiety disorder as primary cause since symptoms predate stress and occur independent of mood state.

doctor.intent: Assess another core inattentive-ADHD symptom: avoidance or reluctance to engage in tasks requiring sustained mental effort
doctor.question: Do you find yourself avoiding, putting off, or dreading tasks that require a lot of sustained mental effort—like paperwork, detailed reports, or planning—even when you know they’re important?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about avoiding or dreading tasks that require sustained mental effort, but the provided symptom profile does not include an item for avoidance of sustained mental effort.

patient.answer:
I don’t know if I’d call it dreading exactly. I mean, paperwork is never my favorite thing, but whose is, right? My sister actually likes forms, which I’ve never understood—she’ll sit there with little folders and labels and everything.

For me, I guess if something looks like it’s going to take a lot of thinking, I might kind of circle around it before I start, but I’m not sure if that’s avoiding it or just… trying to get myself ready. Sometimes I tell myself I’ll do it after one other thing, and then the day gets away from me.

But I don’t know. I wouldn’t say I’ve really noticed it as a pattern, if that’s what you mean.

Were you asking like insomnia, or waking up a lot, or something else? Because I’d have to think about it more. I haven’t really noticed a clear pattern.

doctor.intent: Assess whether inattentive symptoms cause significant impairment across multiple settings (a DSM-5 criterion for ADHD), beyond just work
doctor.question: Would you say these attention and forgetfulness issues have also caused noticeable problems in your relationships or social life—like friends or family feeling frustrated with you for forgetting things or not following through?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: The problems have turned into a serious work issue now: I have a backlog, tenant complaints, and a safety review on my record, and I’m scared it may cost me the promotion path I’ve been working toward.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the attention and forgetfulness symptoms are causing noticeable impairment in life functioning, which most directly matches the functional impairment item.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, socially, I’m not sure that’s where I’d say it shows the most. My family gets annoyed sometimes, sure, but the bigger thing right now is work.

It’s gotten kind of serious there. I’ve got this backlog that keeps following me around, and tenants have been complaining because things don’t get finished or followed up on the way they’re supposed to. And now there’s a safety review on my record, which… I hate even saying that out loud.

I’ve been trying to move up, you know, not stay in the same maintenance role forever, and I’m scared this is going to mess up the promotion path I’ve been working toward. So maybe that’s not exactly what you asked about friends and family, but that’s the part that’s really causing problems.

inference.note: Confirmed multiple domains of inattentive symptoms (distractibility, difficulty organizing, forgetfulness) present since childhood, causing impairment across work and home settings, with no clear evidence of mood, anxiety, sleep, or substance-related explanation. Hyperactive-impulsive symptoms remain absent, consistent with predominantly inattentive presentation.

doctor.intent: Rule out substance use (alcohol, drugs, or excessive caffeine) as a contributing factor to inattentiveness before confirming ADHD diagnosis
doctor.question: Do you regularly drink alcohol, use any recreational drugs, or consume a lot of caffeine, and do you think any of that might be affecting your focus or memory?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about alcohol, recreational drug use, and caffeine as possible alternative explanations for focus or memory problems, but the provided symptom profile does not include substance use, caffeine use, or related rule-out information.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so? I mean, I’m not really sure what counts as “a lot” of caffeine. I’ll have coffee, but then some days at work somebody brings one of those huge gas station cups and everybody acts like that’s normal, so I don’t know where the line is.

Alcohol… I wouldn’t say it’s something I’ve connected to my focus. Recreational drugs, no—well, I mean, not like something that’s part of my life. I haven’t really sat down and compared “this day I drank coffee” to “this day I forgot things,” if that’s what you mean.

My focus problems feel like they’re just kind of there, but I don’t know. Maybe I should pay more attention to that.

inference.note: Substance use, caffeine, and sleep issues do not appear to explain the chronic inattentive symptoms, which have been present since childhood and persist across contexts. No evidence of hyperactive-impulsive symptoms supports predominantly inattentive presentation. Mood/anxiety ruled out as primary cause since inattentiveness predates situational stress.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the inattentive symptoms were present and causing impairment before age 12, as required for ADHD diagnosis, by getting a concrete example of academic or functional impact in childhood
doctor.question: Can you recall a specific instance from before you were about 12 years old—like a missed homework assignment or a forgotten school project—where this kind of forgetfulness actually caused a real consequence, like a bad grade or getting in trouble?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: I remember being this way back in grade school, long before any of this job pressure—teachers said I was bright but always misplaced papers, missed parts of directions, and needed reminders to finish classwork.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for evidence that the forgetfulness and attention problems were present before age 12, with a childhood example and consequence.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I can remember that kind of thing from grade school. I don’t know if I can pull up one perfect example with the exact grade and teacher, but I remember teachers saying I was bright, like I understood things, but I was always losing papers or forgetting to turn things in.

There were times I’d do part of an assignment and miss a whole section because I didn’t catch all the directions, and then I’d get marked down or have to stay in at recess or something to finish it. And I remember needing reminders to finish classwork, like I’d just… not get it completed unless someone came back around and told me to keep going.

It’s funny, I can picture the desks and those paper folders more than the actual assignment. I was always cramming loose papers into them and then somehow the one I needed would disappear. But yeah, this was way before work stress or anything like that. It was back in school.

inference.note: Patient confirmed a specific pre-age-12 example of inattentive symptoms causing real consequences (incomplete assignments, losing papers, needing reminders), supporting childhood onset criterion for inattentive-type ADHD. No hyperactive/impulsive symptoms endorsed, and mood, sleep, and substance use do not better explain the chronic inattentive pattern. Diagnosis remains ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation.
